sections.h: Prayer and sacrifice for the dead in 2 Maccabees 12
sections.b:
After a battle in 163 BC, Judas's men found charms of the idols of Jamnia under the tunics of the fallen. They prayed that the sin be "wiped away entirely", and Judas sent two thousand drachmas to Jerusalem for a sin offering. The writer adds that Judas did this because he believed in the resurrection: "That is why he had atonement made for the dead, to free them from the sin" (2 Maccabees 12:45). It is one of the oldest clear statements that the living can do something for the dead (Doran).

The Catholic Church cites it for purgatory and prayer for the dead (Catechism 1032; Council of Trent, session 25). The Orthodox pray for the dead and use the passage, but Mark of Ephesus argued at the council of Ferrara-Florence (at Ferrara, 1438) that it shows forgiveness through prayer, not a purgatorial fire. Luther at Leipzig (1519) denied that the book could settle a dispute because it is not in the canon; Calvin held the offering "not free from superstition" (Institutes 3.5.8); the Thirty-Nine Articles reject "the Romish Doctrine concerning Purgatory" (Article XXII). Jewish practice came to help the dead through charity and Yizkor on Yom Kippur and the mourner's Kaddish, without citing this book.

sections.h: The dead who pray: Onias and Jeremiah
sections.b: Before his last battle Judas dreamed of the murdered high priest Onias praying with outstretched hands for the whole Jewish people, and of Jeremiah, "the one who prays much for the people and the holy city" (2 Maccabees 15:14). Catholic and Orthodox teaching cites the dream for the intercession of the saints. The Lutheran Apology grants that the saints pray for the church in general but rejects invoking them; Reformed and Anglican confessions reject invocation of saints. The dream shows the dead praying; it does not show anyone asking them to.

2 Maccabees 14:37–46 tells how Razis, an elder of Jerusalem called "father of the Jews", killed himself rather than be taken by Nicanor's soldiers: he fell on his sword, threw himself from a wall, and at last tore out his bowels, praying that God would give them back to him. The writer praises the death as noble. When the Donatists of North Africa cited Razis to defend members who killed themselves, Augustine answered that the deed is told, not praised: Razis was "not wise in choosing death" but "impatient in bearing humiliation" (Letter 204; Against Gaudentius 1). Aquinas called it a weakness of soul unable to bear suffering (Summa II-II 64.5). Protestant critics of the book cited the praise of Razis against its inspiration. Jewish law forbids suicide, though it honors those who died to avoid being forced into sin.

The book that begins with Onias III's godliness (2 Maccabees 3:1) and tells of his murder (4:34) brings him back at the end: in Judas's dream he stands with hands outstretched, praying for the whole Jewish community, and introduces Jeremiah (2 Maccabees 15:12–14). The description repeats the Greek ideal of the "noble and good" man: modest, gentle, well spoken, schooled in virtue from boyhood. Menelaus, who had Onias killed, meets his own end in a tower of ash at Beroea (2 Maccabees 13:3–8), and Josephus says Alcimus followed him as high priest.

2 Maccabees 15:36 sets Nicanor's Day on 13 Adar, "one day before Mordecai's Day". This is the oldest reference to Purim outside Esther, and it calls the feast by Mordecai's name. In Esther the Jews defeat their enemies on 13 Adar and rest on the 14th (Esther 9:17); Judas's victory over Nicanor on the same date made it a second day of deliverance. 1 Maccabees 7:49, Josephus and the Scroll of Fasts also record Nicanor's Day. It lapsed with the Scroll of Fasts; 13 Adar is now the Fast of Esther, first attested in geonic times.

The people voted to keep 13 Adar each year in memory of Judas's victory over Nicanor in 161 BC (2 Maccabees 15:36; 1 Maccabees 7:49). The Scroll of Fasts lists it among the days on which fasting was forbidden, and the Babylonian Talmud tells the story (Ta'anit 18b). Like Hanukkah, it was a feast decreed by the people, not commanded in the Torah; unlike Hanukkah, it did not survive.

The writer explains Judas's sin offering for the dead by the resurrection: "if he had not expected the fallen to rise again, it would have been pointless and silly to pray for the dead" (2 Maccabees 12:44). Razis, dying, calls on the Lord of life to give him back his body (14:46), as the third brother hoped to receive his hands back (7:11). The book holds a bodily resurrection for the faithful, and it is one of the earliest texts to link that hope with prayer for the dead. Paul's question about those "baptized for the dead" (1 Corinthians 15:29) uses the same kind of argument.

2 Maccabees likes punishments that match the crime. Menelaus, who sinned at the altar "whose fire was pure, and its ash too", dies in a tower of ash (2 Maccabees 13:8). Nicanor stretches out his hand against the temple and swears to level it (14:33); after his death his head and hand are shown in Jerusalem and his tongue is fed to the birds (15:30–33). Even the Jewish soldiers who wore idol charms fall in battle (12:40). The pattern runs through the book (4:38; 5:10; 9:5–6).

2 Maccabees 13–15 covers the brief reign of the boy king Antiochus V Eupator (164–162 BC), ruled by his regent Lysias, and the first years of Demetrius I Soter (162–150 BC), who escaped from Rome and had them killed. The book tells of Antiochus V's invasion and hasty peace (2 Maccabees 13), compare 1 Maccabees 6:18–63, and of Demetrius's governors Alcimus and Nicanor (2 Maccabees 14–15), compare 1 Maccabees 7. It adds the execution of Menelaus at Beroea, confirmed by Josephus.

sections.h: From the treaties to Nicanor's defeat
sections.b: 2 Maccabees 12–15 runs from 163 to 161 BC: Judas's raids on Joppa and Jamnia and his campaign in Gilead (compare 1 Maccabees 5), the invasion of Antiochus V and the peace that followed (compare 1 Maccabees 6), and the struggle with Alcimus and Nicanor ending in the victory of 13 Adar (compare 1 Maccabees 7). 2 Maccabees leaves out Judas's defeat at Beth-zechariah and ends before his death at Elasa (1 Maccabees 9:1–18), so the book closes on the temple saved and a feast founded.

In 2 Maccabees 14:6 Alcimus tells Demetrius that "the Jews they call Hasideans, led by Judas Maccabeus" keep the war going. 1 Maccabees instead has the Hasideans seek peace with Alcimus, who kills sixty of them (1 Maccabees 7:12–17). The two passages are central to the debate over whether the Hasideans were a distinct party or the pious supporters of the revolt in general.

sections.h: A good angel before the army
sections.b: Before the battle with Nicanor, Judas recalls the angel who struck Sennacherib's camp (2 Kings 19:35) and asks God to "send a good angel ahead of us" (2 Maccabees 15:23), as God had promised to send an angel before Israel (Exodus 23:20). No angel is seen in the battle; the writer credits the victory to God's care (15:27).

2 Maccabees ends with the writer's own voice: "If it is well written, and its arrangement hits the mark, that is what I myself was hoping for. If it is thin and middling, that was all within my reach" (2 Maccabees 15:38). Calvin argued that a writer who asks pardon is no oracle of the Holy Spirit (Institutes 3.5.8); the Latin he knew does ask pardon, the Greek only admits limits. Catholic and Orthodox writers answer that God inspires human authors with their own labor and style (Dei Verbum 11), as Luke describes his research (Luke 1:1–4).

The fallen soldiers of 2 Maccabees 12:40 wore under their tunics objects consecrated to the idols of Jamnia, probably charms taken as loot. The law forbade keeping the things of idols (Deuteronomy 7:25–26), and the writer counts this as the reason they died, as Achan's hidden plunder caused Israel's defeat at Ai (Joshua 7).

Judas's men bring the fallen home to their family tombs (2 Maccabees 12:39), while Menelaus dies "without even being given earth for a grave" (13:7) and Nicanor's tongue is given to the birds (15:33). Proper burial and its denial mark the righteous and the wicked throughout 2 Maccabees (5:10; 9:28).

Nicanor plans to attack on the Sabbath, expecting no resistance, and mocks the Jews in his army who ask him to honor the day: is there a Sovereign in heaven who commanded it? "And I am a sovereign on earth" (2 Maccabees 15:5). His plan fails. Earlier Judas's men purify themselves and keep the Sabbath at Adullam before recovering the dead (12:38).

sections.h: Nicanor's threat and the priests' prayer
sections.b: Nicanor swears to level the temple and build one to Dionysus unless Judas is handed over (2 Maccabees 14:33). The priests pray to the Lord who "lack nothing" yet chose "to have a temple for your dwelling among us" (14:35), and ask him to keep the house undefiled. After Nicanor's death the people bless God "who has kept his own place free from defilement" (15:34). Compare 1 Maccabees 7:33–38 and Solomon's prayer (1 Kings 8:27).

Before his last battle Judas tells his army "a dream that deserved belief" (2 Maccabees 15:11): Onias praying for the people and Jeremiah handing him a golden sword from God. Greek historians often reported a general's dream before battle; here it gives the outnumbered army confidence that the righteous dead and God stand with them.
